content: Further research is ongoing, but currently, there is insufficient data to establish minimum or maximum concentrations of minerals in drinking water. Adequate intake depends on various factors, and therefore, no guideline values are proposed at this time. Heptachlor and Heptachlor Epoxide Heptachlor (CAS No. 76-44-8) is a broad-spectrum insecticide whose use has been banned or restricted in many countries. Its primary current application is for termite control through subsurface soil injection. Heptachlor is persistent in soil, where it is primarily converted to its epoxide form, heptachlor epoxide (CAS No. 1024-57-3), which is highly resistant to further degradation. Both heptachlor and its epoxide bind strongly to soil particles and migrate very slowly. However, intake has significantly decreased due to reduced usage. In 1991, the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classified heptachlor as Group 2B (possibly carcinogenic to humans) based on sufficient evidence in animals but inadequate evidence in humans. Despite this, concentrations in drinking water are well below levels of health concern, and no formal guideline value is deemed necessary. Hexachlorobenzene (HCB) Hexachlorobenzene (CAS No. 118-74-1) was historically used as a seed dressing to prevent fungal growth in crops but is now primarily a by-product of chemical processes or an impurity in some pesticides. HCB is highly mobile, resistant to degradation, and bioaccumulates in organisms due to its physicochemical properties and slow elimination. It is commonly detected at low levels in food and ambient air. IARC has classified HCB as Group 2B (possibly carcinogenic to humans) based on evidence of tumor induction in three animal species at various sites. A health-based value of 1 µg/L can be derived for HCB in drinking water using a low-dose extrapolation model. However, concentrations in food and water have been steadily declining, and HCB is listed under the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants. As such, no formal guideline value for HCB in drinking water is considered necessary. Hexachlorobutadiene (HCBD) Hexachlorobutadiene (HCBD) is used as a solvent in chlorine gas production, a pesticide, and an intermediate in rubber manufacturing. It has been detected in effluents from chemical plants at concentrations up to 6 µg/L and is also found in air and food. HCBD is easily absorbed and metabolized via conjugation with glutathione, forming a nephrotoxic derivative. IARC classifies HCBD as Group 3 (not classifiable as to its carcinogenicity to humans). Concentrations in drinking water can be controlled by limiting HCBD content in products that come into contact with water. A guideline value of 0.001 mg/L is achievable using granular activated carbon (GAC) treatment. Hydrogen Sulfide Hydrogen sulfide is formed when sulfides are hydrolyzed in water but is usually present at low levels in drinking water due to oxidation in well-aerated or chlorinated water. While hydrogen sulfide gas is highly toxic when inhaled, oral toxicity data are lacking. It is unlikely that harmful doses could be consumed through drinking water. Consequently, no guideline value is proposed. However, hydrogen sulfide can affect the taste and odor of water, making it detectable even at low concentrations. Drinking water is not a significant source, with levels typically below 1–2 µg/L. Tin and its inorganic compounds are poorly absorbed in the gastrointestinal tract, do not accumulate in tissues, and are rapidly excreted. Long-term studies in animals have shown no evidence of carcinogenicity, teratogenicity, or fetotoxicity. Acute gastric irritation is the main adverse effect of excessive tin levels in canned food. The Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA) established a provisional tolerable weekly intake (PTWI) of 14 mg/kg body weight. Due to its low toxicity, tin in drinking water does not pose a health hazard, and no guideline value is necessary. Iodine Iodine occurs naturally in water as iodide and is occasionally used for water disinfection in emergency situations. Iodine is essential for thyroid hormone synthesis, with recommended daily intakes ranging from 90 µg/day for infants to 200 µg/day for pregnant or lactating women. However, data are insufficient to establish a dose-response relationship or a guideline value for iodine in drinking water. Iron Iron is one of the most abundant metals in the Earth's crust and is essential for human nutrition. Drinking water may contain iron due to natural sources, the use of iron coagulants, or corrosion of pipes. Iron levels in drinking water are generally not of health concern, as iron is poorly absorbed and rapidly excreted. The taste and appearance of water are usually affected at levels below those of health concern. No guideline value for iron in drinking water is proposed. Lead Lead is primarily used in lead-acid batteries, solder, and alloys. Its use in petrol and food processing has significantly declined, leading to lower concentrations in air, food, and blood. Lead in drinking water mainly arises from plumbing materials, such as lead pipes and solder. Infants and children are the most sensitive populations, with neurodevelopmental effects being the most concerning. JECFA has withdrawn the PTWI for lead, as no safe threshold for its effects has been identified. A provisional guideline value of 10 µg/L is maintained for drinking water, based on treatment performance and analytical achievability. Lindane Lindane (γ-hexachlorocyclohexane) is an insecticide used on crops, in forestry, and as a therapeutic pesticide. Its use has been restricted in many countries. Lindane is toxic to the liver and kidneys in animal studies but does not induce carcinogenic responses in rats or dogs. It has been associated with liver tumors in certain mouse strains but not in others. Concentrations in food and water have been declining, and a guideline value of 1 µg/L is achievable using granular activated carbon treatment.
